systems.name: International Fixed Calendar
systems.summary: Moses B. Cotsworth’s perennial calendar, first presented in 1902: thirteen 28-day months that all start on a Sunday, with Sol inserted between June and July. Promoted by the International Fixed Calendar League (founded 1923) with George Eastman’s backing and considered by the League of Nations’ calendar-reform inquiries of the 1920s and 1930s, it was used internally at Eastman Kodak from 1928 to 1989.

history.text: Moses B. Cotsworth first presents his 13-month International Fixed Calendar.
The International Fixed Calendar League is founded with George Eastman’s backing, after a League of Nations calendar-reform inquiry rates the plan the best of some 130 proposals.
Eastman Kodak adopts the calendar for its internal business use.
The plan fails to win final approval from the League of Nations, and the IFC League winds down.
Eastman Kodak stops using the calendar, after 61 years.

months.name: Sol
months.meaning: Latin for “sun”: the inserted month sits mid-year, near the northern summer solstice.

intercalaryDays.name: Leap Day
intercalaryDays.description: Follows June 28 in leap years (always Gregorian 17 June). It belongs to no month and has no weekday.

intercalaryDays.name: Year Day
intercalaryDays.description: Follows December 28 (always Gregorian 31 December). It belongs to no month and has no weekday.

systems.name: Positivist Calendar
systems.summary: Auguste Comte’s 1849 calendar of thirteen 28-day months, each named after a figure he considered a great contributor to humanity and each starting on a Monday. Years are counted from the French Revolution: 1789 is year 1.

history.text: The French Revolution begins; Comte later makes 1789 year 1 of the Positivist era.
Auguste Comte proposes the Positivist calendar: 13 months named after great contributors to humanity, plus festival days.

intercalaryDays.name: Festival of All the Dead
intercalaryDays.description: The complementary day after Bichat 28 (Gregorian 31 December, or 30 December in leap years). It belongs to no month and has no weekday.

intercalaryDays.name: Festival of Holy Women
intercalaryDays.description: Follows the Festival of All the Dead in leap years (always Gregorian 31 December). It belongs to no month and has no weekday.

gregorianCalendar.name: Gregorian calendar
gregorianCalendar.summary: The reform of the Julian calendar promulgated by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582: twelve months of 28 to 31 days and a leap day every fourth year, except in centuries not divisible by 400. It is today’s international civil calendar.

history.text: Pope Gregory XIII’s bull Inter gravissimas reforms the Julian calendar; Thursday 4 October is followed by Friday 15 October.
Great Britain and its colonies adopt the Gregorian calendar, skipping 3 to 13 September.
Greece becomes the last European country to adopt it for civil use.
